Ventilated Patients With COVID-19 in Intensive Care Unit 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月09日 来源:Journal of Medical Virology 3.7 编辑推荐: 摘要:重症监护室(ICU)接受机械通气的患者,特别是感染严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2型(SARS-CoV-2)的患者,极易发生单纯疱疹病毒(HSV)再激活。鉴于缺乏关于SARS-CoV-2 Omicron和Delta变异株的数据,本研究旨在评估SARS-CoV 10x Genomics Xenium 原位蛋白检测技术开启空间多组学新维度,立即索取技术资料>> 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 RESEARCH ARTICLE Open Access 摘要:重症监护室(ICU)接受机械通气的患者,特别是感染严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2型(SARS-CoV-2)的患者,极易发生单纯疱疹病毒(HSV)再激活。鉴于缺乏关于SARS-CoV-2 Omicron和Delta变异株的数据,本研究旨在评估SARS-CoV-2肺炎机械通气患者肺部HSV再激活的发生率。研究人员同时研究了HSV复制对SARS-CoV-2复制的影响及其反向作用,以及HSV毒株对抗病毒治疗的敏感性。这项回顾性研究纳入了里昂381例ICU机械通气患者。总体而言,103例患者(27.0%)发生了HSV再激活,其中SARS-CoV-2阳性患者的再激活发生率(32.8%)高于SARS-CoV-2阴性患者(24.1%;p值=0.058)。Delta变异株感染者的HSV再激活率(46.2%)显著高于Omicron感染者(27.1%;p值=0.045);Delta变异株与HSV再激活风险增加2.38倍相关。HSV阳性患者的SARS-CoV-2病毒载量比HSV阴性患者低1个对数级,这一发现表明这是SARS-CoV-2感染的自然病程随后发生HSV再激活,而非病毒干扰所致。出乎意料的是,在HSV载量超过105拷贝/mL的患者中,至少13.6%的HSV-1毒株的UL23基因出现了阿昔洛韦耐药突变。通过互补的表型和基因型方法,研究人员在UL30中鉴定出三个新的氨基酸替换:Q217R、D741A和E756K,这些被归类为多态性。对于发生肺部HSV再激活的ICU机械通气患者,其管理策略仍需进一步优化,尤其是在抗病毒耐药性检测方面。 论文解读:重症监护室COVID-19有创机械通气患者肺部单纯疱疹病毒再激活研究 观看单细胞测序入门大讲堂录播视频&资料下载领 取 一、研究背景与目的 重症监护室(ICU)中接受有创机械通气的患者,无论是免疫抑制还是免疫功能正常的个体,均易发生下呼吸道单纯疱疹病毒(HSV)再激活。HSV在下呼吸道中的检出率可达约64%,且其再激活与机械通气时间延长相关。然而,HSV究竟是疾病进展的致病因素还是潜在疾病的标志物,学术界仍存争议。早期COVID-19大流行期间,HSV是SARS-CoV-2肺炎有创通气患者中最主要的呼吸道病毒共病原体,且常与曲霉菌感染并发。已有研究表明,相较于其他危重患者,SARS-CoV-2相关急性呼吸窘迫综合征(ARDS)患者中HSV再激活更为常见。然而,现有研究主要集中在Alpha和Beta变异株流行时期,针对Omicron和Delta变异株背景下肺部HSV再激活的系统性数据十分匮乏。因此,本研究旨在评估2022年期间因Omicron和Delta变异株导致SARS-CoV-2肺炎的机械通气患者中肺部HSV再激活的发生率,同时探讨SARS-CoV-2感染对HSV复制的影响,以及在ICU相关免疫抑制背景下HSV毒株对抗疱疹药物的敏感性。 二、研究方法概述 这是一项单中心回顾性研究,于2022年1月1日至12月31日在法国里昂市民众救济院(Hospices Civils de Lyon)的三个ICU中进行。研究对象为381例接受有创机械通气的成年患者,所有患者均进行了下呼吸道标本(LRTs)的SARS-CoV-2和HSV聚合酶链反应(PCR)检测。研究收集了人口统计学、临床、微生物学和细胞病理学数据。病毒载量通过逆转录定量PCR(RT-qPCR)测定,并以每106个细胞中的病毒拷贝数进行标准化。HSV耐药性检测采用下一代测序(NGS)技术对UL23和UL30基因进行基因型分析,并通过中性红染料摄取试验进行表型分析。SARS-CoV-2的系统发育分析基于GISAID数据库序列。统计分析采用逻辑回归和线性回归模型。 三、研究结果 3.1 研究人群特征 在381例纳入患者中,128例(33.6%)为SARS-CoV-2阳性。总体人群中,103例(27.0%)发生HSV再激活。SARS-CoV-2阳性患者的HSV再激活率为32.8%(42/128),而阴性患者为24.1%(61/253),差异呈边缘显著性(p=0.058)。两组患者在年龄、性别、入院简化急性生理评分II(SAPS II)及基础免疫抑制比例方面无显著差异。值得注意的是,HSV阳性组中血液系统恶性肿瘤的比例(7.8%)低于HSV阴性组(16.5%)。 3.2 HSV再激活情况 所有HSV阳性LRTs均为HSV-1型,未检测到HSV-2型。在可进行分型的109例SARS-CoV-2阳性患者中,70例(64.2%)感染Omicron变异株,其中19例(27.1%)HSV阳性;39例(35.8%)感染Delta变异株,其中18例(46.2%)HSV阳性。Delta变异株感染者的HSV再激活率显著高于Omicron感染者(p=0.045)。多变量逻辑回归分析显示,仅感染Delta变异株与HSV再激活风险独立相关,其风险是Omicron感染者的2.38倍(95%置信区间[1.01, 5.65];p=0.048)。此外,HSV再激活与患者的免疫状态无关。 3.3 HSV与SARS-CoV-2病毒载量 在共感染的29例患者中,HSV和SARS-CoV-2病毒载量均完成标准化。虽然未达到统计学显著性,但SARS-CoV-2阳性患者的标准化HSV病毒载量呈现低于阴性患者的趋势(p=0.055)。多变量线性回归模型发现,两个变量与HSV复制独立相关:接受体外膜肺氧合(ECMO)治疗的患者HSV复制水平显著更高(β=2.8, 95%置信区间[0.74, 4.80];p=0.010);而较高的SARS-CoV-2标准化病毒载量与较低的HSV复制显著相关(β=?0.50, 95%置信区间[?0.87, ?0.13];p=0.010)。反之,HSV阳性患者的SARS-CoV-2标准化病毒载量显著低于HSV阴性患者(β=?0.89, 95%置信区间[?1.70, ?0.10];p=0.028)。 3.4 抗疱疹病毒耐药性检测 在22例符合测序条件的患者中,15例首次LRTs获得可解读序列。第二次LRTs分析显示,3例(13.6%)患者在UL23基因上携带明确的耐药突变(R51W、R220H或183位点胞嘧啶插入)。另有2例患者携带意义不明的替换(P84Q和Q104H),其位置已知与阿昔洛韦(ACV)耐药相关,若将其计入,耐药率可能高达22.7%。表型分析将UL30基因上的三个新替换Q217R、D741A和E756K归类为天然多态性,而T54K和M228V仍为意义不明。 四、讨论与结论 本研究发现,在Omicron主导的2022年期间,ICU中SARS-CoV-2阳性患者的HSV再激活发生率(32.8%)与既往报道一致。重要的是,这是首个比较Delta与Omicron变异株感染者间HSV再激活率的研究,结果显示Delta变异株感染者的HSV再激活风险是Omicron的2.38倍。这可能归因于Delta变异株更强的肺部嗜性,导致更严重的下呼吸道感染,从而为HSV再激活创造了更有利的环境。鉴于Delta变异株目前已不流行,这一发现提示Omicron变异株的流行可能带来了更少的肺部HSV再激活事件。 研究未观察到直接的病毒干扰现象。HSV阳性患者中SARS-CoV-2病毒载量降低1个对数级,更可能反映了SARS-CoV-2感染的自然病程——即原发感染消退后HSV随之再激活,这可能是SARS-CoV-2诱导的免疫失调的标志。ECMO与更高HSV病毒载量的关联虽具统计学意义,但因病例数极少(仅6例),需谨慎解读,尚不能确定因果关系。 一个关键发现是,在HSV高载量患者中,至少13.6%的毒株出现了ACV耐药突变,甚至可能高达22.7%。这一耐药率与一般免疫抑制人群相当,凸显了ICU患者作为继发性免疫抑制人群的特点,也强调了对此类高风险人群进行系统性HSV药物敏感性筛查的必要性,尤其在治疗开始后的第7天左右。 本研究存在若干局限性:缺乏COVID-19症状发作的时间数据,未进行纵向随访以评估病毒干扰;细胞病理学诊断仅在少数患者中实施,可能导致支气管肺炎的真实患病率被低估。 结论:本研究揭示了SARS-CoV-2变异株(尤其是Delta)在增加ICU患者HSV再激活风险中的潜在作用。观察到的模式符合原发SARS-CoV-2感染后继发HSV再激活的时序,使得病毒载量的解读变得复杂。ECMO相关的发现属于探索性结果,需在大规模队列中验证。高抗病毒耐药率进一步强调了对易产生耐药的ICU患者进行系统性HSV药物敏感性评估的必要性。 打赏 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 records.content: Latest News Singapore Community Crime Education Environment Finance General Elections Health Housing Politics Social Issues Sports Transport International People Tributes Blunder Board Opinion Commentary MS Mail MS Speaks Lifestyle Deals Events Food Places Things To Do Entertainment Branded MS Originals MS Explains MS Features MS Investigates MS Mysteries MS Polls MS Unsolved Videos Latest News Singapore Community Crime Education Environment Finance General Elections Health Housing Politics Social Issues Sports Transport International People Tributes Blunder Board Opinion Commentary MS Mail MS Speaks Lifestyle Deals Events Food Places Things To Do Entertainment Branded MS Originals MS Explains MS Features MS Investigates MS Mysteries MS Polls MS Unsolved Videos 0 Shares Covid-19 vaccines to join national childhood & adult immunisation schedules from 12 Oct Health Latest News Singapore MOH said individuals can consult their doctors about the benefits of vaccination for their specific circumstances. By Prudence Lim - 7 Oct 2026, 6:36 pm Follow us on Whatsapp for the latest updates Follow us on Telegram for the latest updates Covid-19 vaccines remain fully subsidised as vaccination joins national immunisation schedules Covid-19 vaccination will be incorporated into Singapore’s National Childhood Immunisation Schedule (NCIS) and National Adult Immunisation Schedule (NAIS) from 12 Oct. Updated XFG Moderna/Spikevax and XFG Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty vaccines will also be available at more than 600 General Practitioner (GP) clinics, all polyclinics and selected Mobile Vaccination Team (MVT) sites. Source: Heng Swee Keat on Facebook, for illustrative purposes only The Ministry of Health (MOH) and Communicable Diseases Agency announced the changes on Wednesday (7 Oct). Covid-19 vaccination recommended for seniors, medically vulnerable Under the updated national immunisation schedules, Covid-19 vaccination is recommended for: Individuals aged 60 and above Medically vulnerable individuals aged six months and above Residents of aged care facilities Healthcare workers, as well as people living or working with medically vulnerable individuals, are also encouraged to get vaccinated. Other individuals aged six months and above may continue to receive the Covid-19 vaccine if they wish to, MOH said. MOH said individuals can consult their doctors about the benefits of vaccination for their specific circumstances. Picture courtesy of the Ministry of Communications and Information, for illustrative purposes only “As Covid-19 will continue to circulate and pose a risk of severe disease, particularly among older and medically vulnerable individuals, Covid-19 vaccination will be added to the NCIS and NAIS to ensure the vaccine remains accessible and affordable for the public,” MOH said. Updated Covid-19 vaccines available from 12 Oct The updated XFG Moderna/Spikevax and XFG Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty vaccines have been approved by the Health Sciences Authority (HSA). Specifically, the multi-dose vial of Spikevax XFG provides active immunisation for children from six months of age, while the Comirnaty vaccine provides immunisation for individuals 65 years and older. According to MOH, the updated formulations provide better protection against current and emerging Covid-19 strains. Their safety profiles are comparable to previous versions, the ministry said. Source: Spikevax website From 12 Oct, Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty will be available for those aged 12 and above. Moderna/Spikevax will be available for those aged six months and above. Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty will be made available to children aged six months to 11 years from 2 Nov. For those aged six months and above who have previously been vaccinated, an additional dose should be received around one year, and at least five months, after their last vaccine dose. Covid-19 vaccines remain fully subsidised Covid-19 vaccination will continue to be fully subsidised for Singapore Citizens, Permanent Residents, Long Term Pass Holders and certain Short Term Pass Holders. The subsidy applies at participating CHAS GP clinics, polyclinics and MVT sites, until further review. Covid-19 vaccinations will not be claimable under MediSave 500/700, or the MediSave Chronic and Preventive Care scheme from 1 January 2027, until further review. Source: Milovan Dracun’s Images on Canva, for illustrative purposes only More than 600 GP clinics will offer vaccines Appointments at participating GP clinics can be booked through the national vaccination website. People are advised to contact their chosen GP clinic to confirm vaccine availability before visiting. Appointments at polyclinics can be booked through HealthHub. Healthier SG enrollees are encouraged to visit their enrolled clinic for vaccination if it offers Covid-19 vaccination. MVTs will also continue to be deployed across Singapore, particularly to bring vaccination services closer to seniors and residents of aged care facilities. Source: Tan Wu Meng 陈有明 on Facebook, for illustrative purposes only “Covid-19 waves will continue to occur from time to time and can cause severe disease among those who are older or medically vulnerable,” MOH said. “We strongly encourage individuals in the recommended groups to stay up to date with their Covid-19 vaccination, to better protect themselves and those around them.” Also read: MOH rebuts calls by People’s Power Party to suspend Covid-19 vaccinations MOH rebuts calls by People’s Power Party to suspend Covid-19 vaccinations Have news you must share? Get in touch with us via email at news@mustsharenews.com. In half of Republican congressional districts, at least 20% of residents are enrolled in Medicaid, and in half of Democratic districts, at least 25% are enrolled. health in the 2026 Midterms From Drew Altman: A Guide to the Role of Health in the Midterms In a new column, Founding President and CEO Dr. Drew Altman says health care costs are playing a significant role in the midterms as one dimension of voters’ concerns about cost of living, and explains why pollsters, analysts, and candidates should look at it that way, and not as a separate voting issue. He writes, “The ‘issue’ that matters most in this election is cost of living and the cost of health care is a central element of it for voters.” Poll: Cost of Health Care and Gas Top Voters’ Midterm Concerns; Democrats Hold Significant Advantage on Health Care Costs and Cost of Living Health care costs are tied with gas as voters’ top economic concern, and voters trust Democrats more than Republicans on key issues, including health care costs and the cost of living. Meanwhile, support for Medicare-for-All has reached a new high in KFF polling — though views shift significantly when competing claims from critics and proponents are heard. Midterm Election Update: ACA Marketplaces More people than ever got coverage through the Affordable Care Act Marketplaces in 2025, but the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits has driven up what people pay and contributed to declining enrollment in 2026. Law and regulatory changes also tightened ACA eligibility and enrollment requirements. Public opinion of the ACA remains generally favorable, although views remain divided along partisan lines. Belonging Global Presence Home News and Updates COVID-19, Flu, and T1D: How to Stay Safe and Healthy COVID-19, Flu, and T1D: How to Stay Safe and Healthy October 8, 2026 Read more in: Life with T1D Cold and flu season is right around the corner! Being sick is never fun, but for people living with type 1 diabetes (T1D), it poses extra concerns. When a person gets sick, their body is under stress. To combat that stress, the body naturally releases hormones that help fight disease. Those hormones, however, can cause blood-glucose levels in the body to rise and disrupt the way insulin works in the body. As a chronic health condition, T1D is a full-time job. But illness can throw a wrench right through the middle of your management, and people with T1D are at a higher risk of severe complications from the flu, even when their T1D is well managed. Other research has found that people with T1D who were hospitalized due to the flu were more likely to be older, smokers, or had a previous history of heart disease or stroke. There does not appear to be a correlation between T1D and severe complications from COVID-19, but further research is needed—and like all illnesses, a COVID-19 infection places the body under that same level of stress, disrupting the way insulin works and complicating T1D management. That’s why having a sick day plan of action is crucial, especially during cold and flu season! Prevention As the old saying goes, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure—and there’s no better way to be prepared this time of year than getting your annual COVID-19 and flu vaccines! Why do you need a new shot each year? Influenza and COVID-19 are both viruses, and they are evolving constantly as they circulate out in the world. Even though the underlying disease is the same, different strains of COVID-19 and the flu rise and fall over time as they compete with each other to be the most dominant. That’s why scientists and researchers review and update the COVID-19 and flu vaccines every year to target the strains they expect will be circulating. Getting your flu and COVID-19 shot each fall helps ensure that your immune system has the most up to date viral information, in case you get sick—and getting vaccinated early in the season means your immune system has more time to prepare! Find A Vaccine Near You Another way to reduce your chances of getting sick this season? Consider wearing a high-quality, comfortable disposable mask such as a KN-95 or N-95 if you’re spending time in crowded, indoor public spaces where there are likely other sick people—think a city bus, airport terminal, doctor’s office, or pharmacy! Finally, make sure to wash your hands often during cold and flu season, and make sleep and hydration a priority if you’re not feeling well. A mask can also be an asset here, as wearing one if you’re feeling sick but need to venture out helps prevent the spread of illness to others. Preparation Unfortunately, it’s inevitable that you’ll get sick at some point. Luckily, we’ve put together a full sick day guide to help make things a little easier, starting with our sick day checklist: Check Your Blood Sugar Regularly If you’re using a CGM, closely monitor your levels, or check your blood-glucose every 2 to 4 hours with a glucometer. Sick days can cause unexpected spikes or drops in your blood-glucose. Stay Hydrated Drink plenty of fluids—staying hydrated is critical. If you cannot keep fluids down due to vomiting, visit your nearest emergency department immediately. Dehydration can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Don’t Stop Eating It’s important to nibble on some crackers or slowly sip some carbohydrates to prevent ketone development. Your body is already under additional stress from being sick. If you cannot keep food down due to vomiting, visit your nearest emergency department immediately to prevent DKA. Check For Ketones Ketones increase your risk of DKA, which requires intravenous fluids and medical support. If you test positive for moderate or large ketones, call your healthcare team immediately or visit your nearest emergency department. Learn more about ketones. Keep Taking Your Insulin Your body still needs insulin even if you’re eating very little. In some circumstances, your body may need more insulin while it’s fighting off an infection, a fever, or increased inflammation, which can all cause hyperglycemia (high blood sugar). Talk to your healthcare team to help you adjust your insulin doses. Get Emergency Glucagon Have emergency glucagon on hand to treat severe lows and make sure you know how to use it. Today’s single-step emergency glucagon options are easy to use. Ask your doctor for a new prescription and be sure to fill that prescription before you need it. Have Anti-Nausea Medication On Hand Talk with your doctor about a prescription for anti-nausea/antiemetic medication like ondansetron (Zofran) to have on hand for sick days. Have A Sick Day Plan Work with your diabetes care team to develop a plan for managing your T1D while sick. Additionally, many over the counter (OTC) medications can affect blood-glucose levels. Sugar-free cough syrups or cough suppressant pills taken orally are good choices for people with T1D. Other drugs, like decongestants, also raise blood glucose. People with T1D must also be aware of the effects of pain and fever reducers. Acetaminophen, which helps counteract minor aches and fevers associated with the flu or a cold, can cause false or no readings in CGMs and can be toxic to the liver and kidneys. Anyone with kidney complications should speak to their healthcare provider before using these drugs. Ibuprofen should also be administered with care, as it can enhance insulin release and increase the risk of hypoglycemia, or low blood sugar. Finally, here are a few tips on how different illnesses might affect your T1D management needs. Remember to reach out to your healthcare team for support in adjusting insulin doses during sick days! Minor Viruses, Including The Common Cold You may not see much impact on your blood-glucose levels. More severe colds could lead to high blood sugar. If you’re lying low on the couch, the decrease in physical activity can also call for a bit more insulin. Stomach and Respiratory Viruses, Including Norovirus And The Flu Nausea and vomiting complicate T1D management. If you or your loved one can’t keep food down or is vomiting, immediately contact the diabetes care team or seek emergency medical care. Serious Viral Or Bacterial Infections Infections of any kind can lead to high glucose levels. Fevers and infections can mean you may need more insulin, even if you are eating very little. Talk to your healthcare team to adjust insulin doses as needed. Don’t forget: get plenty of fluids and rest, rest, rest! records.content_title: Study Identifies Key Risk Factors for Post-COVID-19 Condition Among Previously Hospitalized Patients | DocWireNews
records.content: This study, published in Frontiers In Public Health, examined the risk factors associated with post-COVID-19 condition among patients who had previously been hospitalized with COVID-19. The study was conducted because individuals who experience severe COVID-19 requiring hospitalization may have a greater risk of developing persistent symptoms and long-term health problems after the acute infection. Key Risk Factors for Post-COVID-19 Condition Among Previously Hospitalized Patients The researchers followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the WHO COVID-19 Global Literature Database for relevant studies published from January 2020 to February 2026. Studies were eligible if they included hospitalized patients with confirmed or probable COVID-19, assessed post-acute outcomes at least 4 weeks after infection or hospitalization, and evaluated potential risk factors. A total of 11 studies were included in the systematic review, and seven provided data suitable for quantitative meta-analysis. The analysis identified five major risk-factor groups: female sex, greater acute disease severity or need for respiratory support, intensive care unit admission, vaccination status, and hypertension. The strongest association was found for greater acute disease severity or advanced respiratory support, which was associated with more than twice the odds of developing post-COVID outcomes (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.77–3.68). Female sex was also associated with increased odds of post-COVID-19 condition (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.60–2.35). ICU admission was associated with higher odds as well (OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.24–2.83), indicating that patients who experienced critical illness may be particularly vulnerable to persistent health problems. In addition, patients who were unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated had increased odds of post-COVID outcomes (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.33–2.72), while hypertension was associated with a more moderate but significant increase in risk (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.16–2.20). The review also reported several additional potential predictors, including obesity, older age, smoking, dysgeusia, greater symptom burden during acute COVID-19, and neurological or psychiatric comorbidities, although evidence for these factors was less consistent. The study suggests that post-COVID-19 condition is particularly associated with the severity of the initial illness and certain patient characteristics. Patients who required advanced respiratory support or ICU care, were unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated, had hypertension, or were female may therefore benefit from closer monitoring after hospital discharge. The authors emphasize that these findings represent associations rather than proof of causation. The conclusions are also limited by the small number of available studies and differences between studies in outcome definitions, follow-up periods, and analytical methods. Nevertheless, the study provides useful evidence for identifying patients at greater risk of post-COVID-19 condition and supports risk-based post-discharge follow-up and continued research using standardized definitions and methods. References Kassymbek S, et al. Front Public Health. 2026 Aug 14;14:1911482. :10.3389/fpubh.2026.1911482

Mina, MD, PhD Author(s)Sabrina McCrear, Michael Mina, MD, PhD Michael Mina, MD, PhD, explains Invivyd's accelerated approval path for VYD2311 and how it could change the timing of COVID-19 protection. Advertisement Invivyd plans to seek accelerated approval for VYD2311 based on neutralizing titer data,1 said Michael Mina, MD, PhD, chief medical officer and chief epidemiologist of Invivyd. In part 2 of this interview with The American Journal of Managed Care® (AJMC®), Mina explains why neutralizing titers are a reasonable surrogate for clinical benefit, giving people more control over how and when they're protected against COVID-19, either alongside or instead of vaccination. This interview has been edited for clarity and length. AJMC: Invivyd plans to pursue a Biologics License Application under the Accelerated Approval Program, based on DECLARATION safety and neutralizing titer data plus LIBERTY. Clinical efficacy data would be unblinded after approval, if granted. Why is neutralizing titer a reasonable basis for approval here, and what would the post-approval confirmatory data need to show? Mina: The neutralizing titers associated with the monoclonal antibody are a terrific surrogate for protection because neutralization by an antibody against a virus is a very direct, almost one-to-one interaction. If you can neutralize the virus, you can stop the virus from growing. In the past, we have actually used our previous data from the same trials I just mentioned, CANOPY and EVADE, to map out what the protective threshold is and how much protection we get given a certain amount of neutralizing antibody titers in the bloodstream. So we can measure the amount of neutralization that's gained from our monoclonal antibody, and we can actually map that using what we call a Cox proportional hazards model to look at how much benefit we believe this is going to equal when it comes to reduction in PCR-confirmed COVID-19 disease. Having that map is very important to us, and it actually enables us to bridge between the surrogate endpoint here, which is the titers, and the expected clinical benefit, which is obviously what patients and providers care about. It's not just our data, too, that gives us such strong belief in neutralization titers as a good surrogate for clinical benefit. Going back to 2020 and 2021, all the way through to today, there have been many different studies, from both monoclonal antibodies and vaccines, that have looked at how much clinical benefit is associated with an ability to neutralize the virus at different levels. There's actually a striking correlation and similarity across studies using all different modalities of immunization that really demonstrate there is a very expected curve, where the higher your neutralizing titers are, the more clinical benefit you're going to gain in terms of a reduction of COVID-19 disease. That very simple mechanism, whereby a neutralizing antibody stops the virus from attaching to human cells and therefore stops it from growing, gives us a lot of confidence that we can take what's been shown in the past and bring it forward into our current state. Now, as you mentioned, we won't be reading out DECLARATION results in terms of clinical benefit, because those events are still accruing, so that's going to be post-accelerated approval. We are aiming to continue the DECLARATION study and event accrual as a confirmatory study, and somewhere down the line, when those events accrue, we will be reading it out. That's something we're in discussion with the FDA about currently. AJMC: Invivyd describes VYD2311 as a vaccine alternative. Which patients do you see it serving: people who can't or won't be vaccinated, people who want added protection alongside vaccination, or both? How might that positioning shape coverage decisions for payers? Mina: Based on the LIBERTY data, we feel quite strongly that this monoclonal antibody will support really anyone who is looking for additional immunological protection against this virus. Nobody is fully immune to the virus, and certainly across the population, we still see people of all different age categories and health categories continue to get sick. Now, that said, we anticipate, and we're looking to have a label that actually matches the vaccine label to a large extent—so individuals who are at high risk for severe disease. That might be individuals over the age of 65 or individuals over 12 with additional comorbidities that could put them at high risk. In terms of how we anticipate people will use it, we actually find the LIBERTY data to be very encouraging, in that this doesn't need to be, "Do I get vaccinated, or do I use a monoclonal?" Right now, we have a situation that is very difficult. We have summer waves, and then those kind of bleed into winter waves. As an epidemiologist, I get a lot of calls from people all the time saying, "Dr. Mina, it's August. Should I get my COVID vaccine? I hear that there's COVID hanging about." I would love to just say, "Yes, go get your COVID vaccine." But the issue is the next sentence I have to say is, "However, the winter wave is probably going to be even bigger, and if you get your COVID vaccine now, it might no longer be giving you much protection by December." So that puts the population in a very challenging position right now: When do they time a vaccine? This is an area where I think a monoclonal antibody has a tremendous opportunity to support. We have now shown in LIBERTY that the combination of a monoclonal with a vaccine does not negatively interact with the vaccine; it actually only positively interacts in terms of reducing the unwanted symptoms of the vaccine. So it drives this question: because there's no immunological penalty, if you will, to getting a monoclonal antibody, there could be a world where people say, "Look, I want protection today in the summer, and I want it in the fall, and then when the winter comes, maybe I want protection from both a monoclonal and a vaccine, so I get both." The existence of choice, and having one of those choices be a passive, direct immunization with a monoclonal, opens up a lot of doors for people to choose how and when they get protected, rather than the current situation, which is, "Do I take this immunological penalty today or later on in terms of getting a vaccine and eliciting a robust immune response? But if I do it now, I don't really want to do it again in a few months." That's the real choice people are currently being faced with. We think that by providing a new modality, we'll actually see a lot of people say, "I want to get one this month and the vaccine later on," or vice versa. Or we may very well see a situation where a physician says to a patient, "Look, if you actually get both of these today, you'll be better protected over the next number of months, and you'll probably have fewer symptoms over the next few days after you get this vaccine if you get the monoclonal with it." So there are a lot of choices to be had in the future, and we're certainly contemplating how we want the label to look as we move forward with the agency. Reference 1. McCrear S. records.content_title: How COVID-19 accelerated advances in metabolic phenotyping
records.content: The cross-sector collaborations that formed during the pandemic have supported metabolic studies into viral pathology and host response, and, in turn, enhanced pandemic preparedness. Image Credit: Corona Borealis Studio/Shutterstock.com The collaborative side of COVID-19 COVID-19 placed significant strain on healthcare systems worldwide and led to more than seven million deaths worldwide. While the long-term effects on health systems, economies, societies, and governance remain substantial, the pandemic also triggered an unprecedented level of scientific, clinical, and industrial partnership. This collaborative effort sped up the development of diagnostics, vaccines, and therapeutics. The International COVID Research Network, as part of the International Phenome Center Network (IPCN), was founded in April 2020 as a rapid international response to research the metabolic effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection through the use of harmonized molecular phenotyping techniques. Drawing on the IPCN’s expertise in population-scale phenotyping, the consortium brought together leading NMR centers and clinical partners to evaluate samples from diverse cohorts and produce comparable data across labs. NMR spectroscopy was chosen as the primary technology due to its ability to provide standardized, reproducible, and rapidly deployable evaluation of both targeted and untargeted metabolic profiles. Bruker BioSpin was a critical supporting partner and co-chair of the Task Force, supplying the common Bruker Avance IVDr (for research use only) NMR analytical platform adopted across participating labs. By coordinating data generation, validation, and scientific exchange, this International COVID Research Network helped provide a more comprehensive understanding of COVID-19 as a systemic disease and enhanced readiness for future pandemic studies. Metabolic phenotyping: A precision lens on disease This collaborative momentum naturally extended into metabolic phenotyping. Using advanced NMR and mass spectroscopy (MS), scientists generated high-density molecular data from biological fluids and tissue samples. These profiles, evaluated via statistical modeling, enabled individual and population-level comparisons to determine critical metabolic signatures of physiological and pathological conditions. 1,2 The ability to map such in-depth biochemical profiles enabled scientists to determine personalized treatment targets and stratify disease risk. 3 These capabilities were especially useful during the pandemic for providing insight into the metabolic impacts of SARS-CoV-2. The structure of the International COVID-19 Research Network team improved this effect. With extensive experience in population phenotyping, 10 long-standing partners (ANPC, CIC-bioGUNE, Tübingen University, University of Lübeck, Graz University, CERM Florence, Trondheim University, Vanderbilt University, Cincinnati Children's Hospital, and Bruker as the supporting partner) efficiently gathered and evaluated small sample sets across clinical sites. Following local processing, data was pooled to improve statistical significance. All labs operated using a shared Bruker Avance IVDr NMR platform, which allowed for standardized targeted and untargeted modeling. This configuration also supported fast cross-validation of novel biomarkers and methodological innovations. This article details the remarkable contributions of the International COVID-19 Research Network to advancing COVID-19 research and summarizes the implications for future research on novel diseases. “COVID-19-driven" metabolic discoveries Lipoproteins: Crucial biomarkers for prognosis, disease outcome, and recovery rate Ensuring complete standardization of sample preparation, NMR measurements, and analysis across the research enabled recording spectra on the same spectrometer type at multiple sites in an archetypal manner. Consequently, spectral data from different sites could be combined for much larger-scale untargeted evaluation. Among the most consistent findings of the consortium was an increase in triglycerides in low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) in patients with acute infection, most likely resulting from both overproduction and impaired clearance. This pattern may contribute to the observed association between COVID-19 and insulin resistance. Even more intriguing, COVID-19 prognosis models demonstrated that lipoproteins provided the best predictive markers of patient outcomes. Lipoproteins measured from serum samples from patients eight to 61 days before death provided a valuable discriminatory marker, distinguishing survivors from non-survivors with severe COVID infection. Metabolic variation during recovery from SARS-CoV-2 infection Another finding of the consortium was that molecular metabolite variations were consistent across populations in Europe and Australia. Hyperglycemia and an abnormal amino acid signature were consistently observed in COVID-19 cohorts. This profile is consistent with a diabetic metabolic profile. 4 Consortium collaborators Holmes et al. and Bizkarguenaga et al. identified heterogeneity in recovery from SARS-CoV-2 infection, with some patients exhibiting biochemical abnormalities even three to six months after the acute infection. 5,6 This recovery research found elevated levels of the inflammatory markers GlycA and/or GlycB in certain individuals. Another research group within the COVID-19 network analyzed serum samples acquired from 263 patients hospitalized following positive PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 infection and identified ketone bodies as a key discriminatory metabolite for SARS-CoV-2 infection. Compromised mitochondrial function was indicated in patients who continued to display elevated ketone and pyruvate levels. Symptoms of fatigue, inability to concentrate, and brain fog were specifically associated with elevated quinolinate (a neurotoxic metabolite) and reduced tryptophan. 7 Methodological developments beyond the pandemic In addition to serum-based evaluations, the consortium also investigated whether urine-based metabolic profiling could deliver complementary, non-invasive insights into SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study demonstrated the feasibility of using urine samples for non-invasive diagnostic and prognostic screening of COVID-19. Compared to healthy control patients, patients with COVID-19 exhibited elevated levels of glucose, acetone, taurine, and lactic acid, while hippuric acid, tartaric acid, and creatine were reduced. Metabolic urinary concentrations could also be used to determine the severity of the infection. 8 Another significant advancement was the development of the J-Edited Diffusional (JEDI) proton NMR spectroscopic technique. JEDI was integrated into Bruker's IVDr platform and employed in Bruker’s PhenoRiskPACS1.0 Data Analysis Module, enabling high-fidelity quantification of critical inflammatory biomarkers Glycoproteins GlycA/B and Supramolecular Phospholipid Composite SPC1-3. Using this technique, these markers are isolated by removing spectral signals from small molecules, large proteins, and specific lipoprotein peaks. Notably, the utility of this method extends well beyond COVID-19. It is also proving valuable for measuring SPC1-3 and GlycA/B for other disease conditions, such as sepsis and obesity. 9,10 Conclusion The study conducted by the International COVID Research Network delivered deeper, more novel insights into the multisystemic organ pathologies of COVID-19 at the metabolite level, including the identification of metabolic compounds that predict viral infection. As a result, researchers provided valuable insights into monitoring patients during SARS-CoV-2 infection and throughout recovery. The consortium's methodological developments deliver more precise and enhanced measurements of lipo- and glycoproteins, while also enabling translation to affordable, field-deployable benchtop NMR spectrometers. Their use of NMR multi-cohort research enabled rapid validation of these techniques. References and further reading Bales, J.R., et al . (1988). About Bruker BioSpin Group The Bruker BioSpin Group designs, manufactures, and distributes advanced scientific instruments based on magnetic resonance and preclinical imaging technologies. These include our industry-leading NMR and EPR spectrometers, as well as imaging systems utilizing MRI, PET, SPECT, CT, Optical and MPI modalities. The Group also offers integrated software solutions and automation tools to support digital transformation across research and quality control environments. Bruker BioSpin’s customers in academic, government, industrial, and pharmaceutical sectors rely on these technologies to gain detailed insights into molecular structure, dynamics, and interactions. Our solutions play a key role in structural biology, drug discovery, disease research, metabolomics, and advanced materials analysis. Recent investments in lab automation, optical imaging, and contract research services further strengthen our ability to support evolving customer needs and enable scientific innovation. Appointments are available at CVS.com, MinuteClinic.com and through the CVS Health® app, and walk-ins are accepted at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic. “We know patients value having convenient access to the vaccines and preventive care services they need,” said Amy Compton-Phillips, MD, Executive Vice President and Chief Medical Officer, CVS Health. “With updated COVID-19 vaccines available at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic, we're making it easier for people to get vaccinated close to home and on a schedule that works for them.” CVS Pharmacy offers COVID-19 vaccinations for eligible patients based on state regulations*, while MinuteClinic provides vaccinations for patients beginning at 18 months of age. Pharmacists and MinuteClinic providers are available to answer questions and help patients make informed decisions about vaccination based on their individual health needs. Flexible scheduling for families and caregivers Vaccination appointments are available seven days a week, including evenings and weekends. Patients can schedule appointments at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic for up to four people at the same time, helping families and caregivers get vaccinated together. If eligible, patients can also receive multiple recommended vaccinations during a single visit, including flu, RSV and other routine immunizations. The updated COVID-19 vaccine is available at no-cost through most insurance plans. For those who are uninsured, the cost at CVS Pharmacy and MinuteClinic varies depending on product type and eligibility. ### About CVS Health CVS Health is a leading health solutions company simplifying health care one person, one family and one community at a time. As of June 30, 2026, the Company had approximately 9,000 retail pharmacy locations, more than 1,000 walk-in and primary care medical clinics and a leading pharmacy benefits manager with approximately 87 million plan members. The Company also serves an estimated 37 million people through a broad range of health insurance products and related services. The Company’s integrated model uses personalized, technology driven services to connect people to simply better health, increasing access to quality care, delivering better outcomes, and lowering overall costs. records.content_title: Researchers find gene expression patterns linked to severe pediatric COVID-19
records.content: Researchers have identified patterns of gene activity associated with severe COVID-19 in children that are shared with other serious respiratory infections. The findings, published in BMC Infectious Diseases , offer early clues to how the immune system responds to severe infections, which children are at higher risk and potential targets for treatment. Lower respiratory tract infections, including COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) are major causes of childhood illness and death, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Researchers from the University of Southampton and the University of Cape Town, together with international partners, have analyzed gene expression in blood samples from 333 children from South Africa. The team compared samples from children hospitalised with severe COVID-19, RSV and PTB infections with those of children with only mild or asymptomatic COVID-19, and a control group of healthy children. They identified more than 5,000 genes being expressed differently in children with severe infections. They also discovered ten groups of genes which were expressed in a similar pattern across the different lower respiratory tract infections. These were linked to immune responses, cell regulation and other biological processes involved in infection. The researchers also identified 82 genes that helped distinguish mild or asymptomatic COVID-19 infection from severe cases, suggesting that gene-expression patterns could potentially be used as an indicator of disease severity. Dr Negusse Kitaba, Senior Research Fellow at the University of Southampton and lead researcher, said: "These findings provide new insights into the biological pathways involved in disease severity and highlight genes for further investigation as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets." Professor Heather Zar, Director of the South African Medical Research Council Unit on Child & Adolescent Health, University of Cape Town, and Principal Investigator of the three studies in South Africa that informed this work, added: "There's been limited research examining biological responses to these infections in African children. There's also been few studies on host gene expression in infants and children with COVID-19 globally, so this study helps to close an important evidence gap." This study highlights the value of international collaboration in understanding childhood respiratory disease and provides a foundation for future research into why some children develop severe infection." Professor John Holloway, Professor of Allergy and Respiratory Genetics, University of Southampton The team say that further research with larger groups of children will be needed to determine whether these promising gene signature discoveries can be developed for clinical use. Source: Journal reference: Kitaba, N. T., et al. (2026). Immune transcriptomic differences in paediatric patients with SARS-CoV-2 compared to other lower respiratory tract infections. BMC Infectious Diseases . DOI: 10.1186/s12879-026-14343-x. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12879-026-14343-x

records.content: Welcome to the University of Cape Town News Wamkelekile, Welkom Menu Search News Daily news Newsbytes Research & innovation Newsletters Publications Lectures & speeches Photo essays Videos Audio Campus communications From the UCT Executive Campus Announcements In remembrance Campus updates Audio Media communications Archives News archives Features archives Campus communication archives Media archives Debates in higher education Contact Us Newsroom Media liaison Social Media UCT-led international study uncovers gene clues to severe COVID-19 in children 09 October 2026 | Story Ridovhona Mbulaheni. Photo iStock. Read time 3 min. Researchers identified 82 genes that helped distinguish mild or asymptomatic SARS-CoV2 infection from severe COVID-19, suggesting that gene-expression patterns could be used as an indicator of disease severity. Researchers from the University of Cape Town (UCT) and the University of Southampton, together with international partners, have identified patterns of gene expression associated with severe COVID-19 in children; patterns that are shared with other serious respiratory infections, as well as patterns that distinguish these illnesses. The findings, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, offer early clues about how the immune system responds to severe lower respiratory tract infection, identify which children are at higher risk and may offer potential targets for treatment. Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) – including COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) – are major causes of childhood illness and death, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. The researchers analysed gene expression in blood samples from 333 children from South Africa. They also compared samples from children hospitalised with severe COVID-19, with those from children with RSV lower respiratory tract infection or PTB. In addition, a healthy group of children were compared, including children with only mild or asymptomatic SARS-CoV2 – the cause of COVID-19 – and a control group of healthy children. Findings They identified more than 5 000 genes expressed differently in children with severe infections. They also discovered 10 groups of genes which were expressed in a similar pattern across the different lower respiratory tract infections. These were linked to immune responses, cell regulation and other biological processes involved in infection. The researchers also identified 82 genes that helped distinguish mild or asymptomatic SARS-CoV2 infection from severe COVID-19, suggesting that gene-expression patterns could be used as an indicator of disease severity. “This study helps to close an important evidence gap.” Professor Heather Zar, principal investigator of this study, and of the Drakenstein Child Health Study – a birth cohort study from which many of the children were included – and chairperson of UCT’s Department of Paediatrics & Child Health, said: “There’s been limited research examining biological responses to these infections in African children. There’s also been few studies on host gene expression in infants and children with COVID-19 as well as other LRTIs globally, so this study helps to close an important evidence gap.” Dr Negusse Kitaba, senior research fellow at the University of Southampton and lead researcher, expressed similar sentiment, highlighting how the findings address the gaps by identifying differences in gene activity associated with disease severity. “These findings provide new insights into the biological pathways involved in disease severity and highlight genes for further investigation as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets,” Dr Kitaba said. The study also points to the value of bringing together expertise and data from different research settings, according to John Holloway, a professor of Allergy and Respiratory Genetics from the University of Southampton. “This study highlights the value of international collaboration in understanding childhood respiratory disease and provides a foundation for future research into why some children develop severe infection,” he said. According to the study, further research with larger groups of children will be needed to determine whether these promising gene signature discoveries can be developed for clinical use. records.content_title: Karl-Anthony Towns Credits COVID-19 Pandemic for Relationship With Now-Wife Jordyn Woods
records.content: Karl Anthony Towns and now-wife Jordyn Woods began dating in 2020 after being friends for years — however, that year would turn out to be the "toughest year" of his life. "During this pandemic, I got closer to Jordyn Woods and this is something that brought us to the point that we are now, which is married," Towns, 30, told People on Tuesday, October 6. "She understands the importance for me to be very protective against COVID-19 because my family and I don't do well and she's seen it firsthand when I did have it." The New York Knicks star, who suffered from asthma, was hospitalized with the viral disease and lost seven family members to the coronavirus, including his beloved mother, Jacqueline . "The matriarch of the Towns family, she was an incredible source of strength; a fiery, caring, and extremely loving person, who touched everyone she met," the Towns family said in a statement following her April 13, 2020, death. "Her passion was palpable and her energy will never be replaced." COVID " broke me down to the core ," Towns told People on Tuesday, "[but] in a way also built me up to the man I am today." Explaining "COVID-19 is still around and it's still affecting millions of people," Towns — who has partnered with the FDA's newest approved COVID-19 vaccine — added, "That is one way to understand why hygiene and this vaccine is so important. On top of that, doctors and pharmacists are here to do the best they can to keep people healthy and living longer and better lives." Towns and Woods married on August 15. The indictment, announced Friday, charges 57-year-old Marc Aaron Potash with conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud and seven counts of healthcare fraud, according to a news release issued by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland. The charges relate to the alleged submission of false and fraudulent medical claims sent to Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (FEHBP) and other insurers for at-home, self-administered COVID-19 tests. The defendant allegedly conspired with others to obtain money through false and fraudulent representations to insurers that were facilitated through his Gaithersburg company, Tiero, LLC. The alleged crimes happened between 2022 and May 2026, the U.S. Attorney's Office said. Potash and others submitted documents that falsely claimed Tiero's medical providers were performing on-site COVID-19 testing at the company's purported lab, the indictment states. Fraudulent claims were then allegedly submitted to insurers that listed false dates of service, a fake place of service, and a phony rendering provider for COVID-19 tests. "However, in reality, Potash and his co-conspirators merely shipped over-the-counter, self-administered COVID-19 tests to insured individuals across the country," the news release said. "In total, Potash and his co-conspirators caused the submission of more than $100 million in false and fraudulent healthcare claims, resulting in more than $50 million in insurance payments to Tiero." The indictment also alleges that Potash engaged in "multiple monetary transactions in criminally derived property." This allegedly included Potash purchasing a Range Rover, Mercedes-Benz, and $4 million in real estate property in Beallsville, Maryland. In addition, two security transfers totaled more than $12 million, the news release said. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE If convicted, Potash faces a maximum of 10 years in federal prison, the U.S. Attorney's Office said. records.content_title: Global trust in science lower than before Covid pandemic, report finds
records.content: The proportion of people expressing at least some trust in science has fallen 5 per cent since 2018 Global trust in science is lower than it was before the Covid-19 pandemic, a new report has found. More than 140,000 people in 140 countries were polled for the third wave of The Wellcome Global Monitor, the world’s largest study into how people regard and feel about science. The proportion of people expressing at least some trust in science was 77 per cent in 2018, rose to 80 per cent in 2020, but then fell to 72 per cent in 2025. People who felt worse off financially, or had less confidence in their countries’ healthcare systems, were also less likely to say they trusted science. Only 21 per cent of respondents in sub-Saharan Africa reported having “a lot” of trust in science, compared with 54 per cent in Western Europe. Low trust levels are likely to have an impact on how health programmes can operate, experts said. “Public trust shapes whether scientific advances can make a meaningful difference in people’s lives,” said John-Arne Røttingen, CEO of Wellcome. “As the world faces increasing challenges, from infectious diseases to climate change and mental health, science has the potential for shaping a healthier future, but only if people trust that it is a force for good.” Despite the global bump in trust during the Covid-19 pandemic, in sub-Saharan Africa as well as Central Asia and Western Asia, there was a steady fall in trust across the three survey waves. And while in Central Asia the trend reflected a gradual softening of views, with more people moving from “a lot” of trust in science to “some” trust, in the other two regions views appeared to harden, with growing proportions saying they trust science either “not much” or “not at all”. A health worker collects a swab sample from a passenger to test for the Covid-19 coronavirus, on arrival at Anna International Airport in Chennai on December 24, 2022. (AFP/Getty) While there was some diversity between countries, overall only 28 per cent of respondents in sub-Saharan Africa felt science benefited “most” people in their country. “Across Africa, people have lived through a series of major shocks and challenges in recent years: rising living costs and economic insecurity, the lasting impacts of Covid-19, rising pressure on health systems, recurring disease outbreaks including mpox, Marburg virus and Ebola , conflict and displacement, and the growing effects of climate change on health,” said Dr Aneesa Ahmed, head of programmes at health NGO Amref Health Africa. “If families are struggling financially, if clinics lack medicines or staff, or if communities feel excluded from decision-making, trust can be affected.” Trust is, however, “fundamental” to health programmes, she said. “Communities may only encounter science through practical experiences such as an immunisation drive, a maternal health outreach clinic, or a local community health worker visit to their home. If people have low trust in the institutions delivering those services, or do not feel that programmes reflect their own priorities and realities, implementation becomes much harder.” The report comes as health systems in many African countries are reeling from the impact of aid cuts by countries like the US and UK, who have historically been major donors. Low trust also helped misinformation to spread, Ahmed added, “especially through social media”. Health authorities working to tackle the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have frequently warned that mistrust and misinformation in local communities is hampering the response. In the DRC, 22 per cent of people reported having “no trust” in science at all. Dr Evelyn Gitau, chief scientific officer, Science for Africa Foundation and part of the report’s steering group, said that poor availability of laboratory tests early in the DRC outbreak had driven that mistrust. “All the interventions that we said would work, were not readily available,” she said, and so while “people knew what they were supposed to do [...] they rejected it because they felt things were taking too long”. She said there were wider issues where people in Africa were not feeling the benefits of research, even in communities that had been part of programmes for decades. “Trust in science is shaped by people’s lived experiences, including whether they can access and benefit from the systems and knowledge that science produces. In Africa, that means asking where research comes from, who leads and funds it, and whether local communities and institutions have ownership of, and benefit from, its results,” she added. “A lot of research, especially health research, has come to Africa, but it has come to Africa more from a north-south kind of gaze, so it’s research for the participants and not necessarily with them.” The fact most scientific research projects were health focused meant that “if our health systems are poor, people are going to really equate that to the fact that science is actually not working for them - and that is the reality, a lot of our health systems are really struggling,” she added. This article was produced as part of The Independent’s Rethinking Global Aid project

Playing in :00 shares Share this Article Share Share via device FacebookXLinkedInWhatsAppRedditEmailCopy Link Staff view 0 shares Comments Hawaiʻi Department of Health encourages residents to take common-sense precautions against influenza, COVID-19 and other respiratory viruses as respiratory virus activity increases throughout the state. Recent surveillance shows influenza activity increased, with 20.3% of specimens testing positive for flu during the week of Sept. 23-30, up from the previous week. The state Health Department also continues to monitor COVID-19 and reports cases began to decrease during the same week. Omicron variant of COVID-19. (File Image: World Health Organization) “Respiratory viruses circulate year-round in Hawaiʻi and we are seeing increased activity as we enter the fall respiratory virus season,” said State Epidemiologist Dr. Sarah Kemble. “Getting recommended vaccines, staying home when you are sick and taking simple precautions around others can help reduce the spread of illness and protect people who are more vulnerable to severe disease.” The West Coast Health Alliance, which includes Hawaiʻi, recently issued its 2026-27 respiratory virus season immunization recommendations. Alliance officials recommend annual flu vaccination for everyone 6 months and older, as well as updated COVID vaccination for specific higher risk populations, including all children ages 6 to 23 months, all adults age 65 years and older and people ages 2 to 64 years with risk factors. West Coast Health Alliance also recommends COVID vaccination for people planning pregnancy, are pregnant or postpartum; for healthcare workers; and other people living or working closely with people at higher risk, and anyone else who chooses vaccination to reduce the risk of severe illness. “People should talk with their healthcare provider about which vaccines are recommended for them and whether they are up to date,” Kemble said. “The updated vaccines are an important tool for reducing the risk of severe illness, particularly for people at higher risk.” State health officials also recommend several straightforward steps to help prevent respiratory illness: Stay home when sick. Stay home until you are fever-free at least 24 hours without using fever-reducing medication and other symptoms are mild and improving. Consider wearing a mask. Masks can provide additional protection, particularly in crowded indoor settings, when respiratory virus activity is high or when spending time around people at higher risk of severe illness. Improve indoor air. Open doors or windows, use air purifiers or gather outdoors when possible. Practice good hygiene. Wash hands regularly and cover coughs and sneezes. Test and seek treatment when appropriate. People at higher risk for severe disease who develop respiratory symptoms should contact their healthcare provider. Antiviral medications for COVID-19 and influenza work best when started as soon as possible. People at increased risk for severe respiratory illness include kūpuna, young children, pregnant people, people with weakened immune systems and people with certain underlying medical conditions. People who live with or regularly care for someone at higher risk can also take additional precautions to reduce the likelihood of spreading illness. Screenshot of image from Hawaiʻi Department of Health email. The state Health Department encourages residents to talk with their healthcare provider about individual vaccination needs and use reliable health information as respiratory virus activity changes. Visit the Hawaiʻi Department of Health respiratory virus resources website for more information about respiratory viruses, COVID-19, influenza and vaccination recommendations. records.content: Catherine Mackinlay Updated Fri, October 9, 2026 at 4:05 PM UTC 0 Health officials have issued an update on the BA.3.2 'Cicada' Covid variant as infections rise (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror) The Government has issued an update on a Covid variant dubbed "Cicada" as coronavirus infections rise across the UK. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said BA.3.2, sometimes referred to as the "Cicada" variant, is a highly divergent descendant of the Omicron BA.3 lineage which re-emerged in South Africa in late 2024. The strain has since been detected sporadically across multiple continents and has been designated a Variant Under Monitoring by the World Health Organisation (WHO). However, health officials stressed that the current public health risk from BA.3.2 is considered low, with no evidence that it causes increased severity, hospitalisation or mortality, although available evidence remains limited. The update comes as another Covid strain, XFG, remains the most common variant currently circulating. XFG, also known as Stratus and dubbed 'American Covid' in some media reports, has been circulating in the UK and elsewhere for around a year. UKHSA data shows Covid positive test rates rose to around seven per cent in September, while hospital admission rates increased by approximately 50 per cent over the same period. The increases have been recorded across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, as well as elsewhere in Europe and the United States. Despite the rise, UKHSA said current data does not indicate that circulating variants are causing more severe illness than other Covid variants. Officials said increases in hospitalisations are broadly in line with the overall rise in Covid circulation, suggesting greater levels of infection rather than a particular variant causing more serious disease. UKHSA said several factors could be contributing to the current increase. Colder and wetter weather means people are spending more time indoors, making it easier for respiratory viruses to spread. It has also been roughly a year since the last significant Covid wave, meaning immunity from previous infections and vaccinations may be waning among parts of the population. People experiencing symptoms of a respiratory infection who have a high temperature or do not feel well enough to carry out their normal activities are advised to stay at home where possible and avoid contact with vulnerable people. The 'Cicada' variant re-emerged in South Africa in late 2024 (Image: Getty) Those who cannot stay at home are advised to wear a well-fitting face covering, avoid crowded or poorly ventilated places and practise good hand and respiratory hygiene. The NHS says Covid symptoms can include a high temperature, cough, shortness of breath, tiredness, headache, sore throat and a blocked or runny nose. UKHSA also stressed that vaccines remain the best defence against severe Covid illness and hospitalisation. People aged 75 and over, those with weakened immune systems and residents of care homes for older people are currently among those eligible for vaccination. UKHSA said it continues to monitor Covid variants using GP appointments, A&E attendances, hospitalisations and genomic sequencing. Hospital data helps officials track more severe cases and assess how quickly different variants are spreading. The agency also publishes weekly surveillance data on Covid and other respiratory illnesses throughout winter. People at the highest risk of becoming seriously ill may be eligible for NHS treatment if they develop symptoms and test positive. This can include people with weakened immune systems, certain cancers, kidney or liver disease and organ transplants. Some people with conditions affecting the lungs, brain or nervous system may also be eligible for treatment

Close Search & Section Navigation News UKUSAsiaFeature Business Entertainment Culture Sports Lifestyle Features National Trust Awards ACTAsAsian Business AwardsEastern Eye Property AwardsEastern Eye Restaurant Awards Trending Power List More ColumnComment More TrendingPower ListColumnComment Follow Us: Home> Lifestyle> Health> XFG 'American Covid" is rising in the UK: What you need to know> Submit Guest Post XFG 'American Covid" is rising in the UK: What you need to know XFG, also known as “Stratus,” is driving a rise in COVID activity across the UK, but health officials say there is no evidence it causes more severe illness. Here’s what the latest numbers, symptoms and vaccine guidance mean. That increase is worth watching, particularly as winter approaches and respiratory viruses generally circulate more widely. iStock By Vibhuti PathakOct 08, 2026 Vibhuti Pathak See Full Bio Highlights: FG is now a major COVID variant in the UK. UK COVID cases and hospital admissions are rising. There is no evidence XFG causes more severe disease. Symptoms remain similar to previous COVID variants. Health officials say there is no need for public panic. COVID-19 is once again making headlines in the UK, with infections and hospital admissions moving upward as autumn sets in. But for most people, the latest rise is a reason to be sensible, not scared. The XFG variant, sometimes called “Stratus” in media reports, is now one of the main SARS-CoV-2 lineages being tracked in the UK and globally. The World Health Organization classifies XFG as a variant under monitoring, while UKHSA says current evidence does not indicate that XFG causes more severe illness than other variants currently circulating. That is an important distinction as social media discussions about a new COVID “strain” can make a rise in cases sound more alarming than the evidence suggests. So, what is XFG? Ask AIHow does the rise of the XFG variant impact British Asian communities, especially those with higher risk factors? XFG is a descendant of the Omicron family of COVID-19 variants. It has become increasingly widespread internationally, with WHO data showing that it accounted for 49% of submitted SARS-CoV-2 sequences globally in the week ending August 23, 2026. Its growing prevalence is one reason health authorities continue to monitor it closely. But being widespread does not automatically mean being more dangerous. UKHSA's assessment remains reassuring: current data do not show that XFG or other currently common variants result in more severe disease. Why are UK cases rising? The latest UKHSA dashboard shows reported COVID cases reaching 1,364 in the seven days to September 23, an increase of 28.6 per cent from the previous seven-day period. Hospital admissions were also rising, reaching 261 in the week to August 31, up 15 per cent. That increase is worth watching, particularly as winter approaches and respiratory viruses generally circulate more widely. But health officials also point out that surveillance figures do not represent every COVID infection. Many people with mild symptoms may never seek medical attention or receive a formal diagnosis. So a rise in reported cases should not be interpreted as evidence that the country is heading back to the conditions seen during the early pandemic. What are healthcare experts saying? The message from public health authorities is essentially: keep an eye on the numbers, but don't panic. Alex Allen, a consultant epidemiologist at UKHSA, previously said that while COVID activity had shown increases, cases remained at low levels in the UK and that the agency was continuing to monitor variants in Britain and overseas. UKHSA's current assessment is similarly measured. Its experts say there is currently no indication that XFG causes more severe illness than other circulating variants. That means the most important question is not simply whether someone has XFG, but whether they are becoming seriously unwell or belong to a group at higher risk of complications. What symptoms should you look for? There is no confirmed symptom that uniquely identifies XFG. The NHS lists common COVID symptoms, including a high temperature, continuous cough, sore throat, blocked or runny nose, tiredness, headache, body aches and shortness of breath. Loss or change of smell or taste can also occur, although it is less characteristic of newer Omicron-lineage infections. Because these symptoms overlap with flu and ordinary respiratory infections, symptoms alone cannot reliably tell you which virus you have. Who needs to be more careful? COVID remains more concerning for older people, immunosuppressed people and others at increased risk of severe disease. The UK's autumn 2026 vaccination programme is specifically targeted at people at highest risk: adults aged 75 and over, residents of older-adult care homes and people aged six months and over who are immunosuppressed. The NHS says vaccination continues to provide protection against severe illness and hospitalisation. For eligible people, the latest UK programme includes an updated XFG-targeted Moderna vaccine for adults and an XFG-targeted Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine for eligible 12- to 17-year-olds. What should you do if you get symptoms? For most otherwise healthy people, the advice is straightforward: rest, drink plenty of fluids and stay home if you have a high temperature or feel too unwell to carry out normal activities. The NHS recommends avoiding contact with other people while you are unwell and taking particular care around people who are more vulnerable to serious infection. People eligible for COVID treatments because they are at particularly high risk should test promptly after developing symptoms, because antiviral treatment needs to be started quickly to be effective. Seek urgent medical advice through NHS 111 if symptoms are worsening or you are concerned. Call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, sudden chest pain, coughing up blood, collapse or other signs of a serious emergency. XFG is spreading, and UK COVID activity is rising. Those developments deserve monitoring, particularly heading into winter. But there is currently no evidence that XFG is a more severe form of COVID, and the UK remains far removed from the extraordinary hospitalisation levels seen during the pandemic's worst periods. UKHSA continues to monitor the variant, while the NHS is focusing vaccination on people most likely to suffer serious complications. For the public, the message is simple: stay informed, know the symptoms, protect vulnerable people around you and take up vaccination if you are eligible but there is no need to panic. american covidcoronavirus ukcovid symptoms 2026covid vaccine ukcovid variant ukcovid winter 2026covid-19 uknhs covid advicerespiratory viruses ukstratus coviduk covid cases 2026uk covid hospital admissionsuk covid vaccinationukhsa covidxfg covid ukxfg covid variantxfg omicronxfg symptomsxfg vaccinexfg variant symptomsxfg covid variant uk Add EasternEye As Your Trusted Source Related News Fitness Why Do Energy Crashes Happen During Workouts? records.content: Home News Screeners Insights ScanXNewsSunshine Biopharma publishes study on MR1-114 efficacy Sunshine Biopharma publishes study on MR1-114 efficacy 1 min read | Published on 20 Jul 2026, 10:35 PM |Updated on 20 Jul 2026, 10:35 PM Reviewed by Riya DScanX News Team Add as a preferred source on Google Key Highlights Sunshine Biopharma Inc. and the University of Arizona published research in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry on MR1-114, a PLpro inhibitor showing nanomolar potency against SARS-CoV-2 variants. The study demonstrated that MR1-114 matched Nirmatrelvir's efficacy in mouse models, suppressing viral replication and preventing weight loss. The compound targets the BL2 groove and cryptic Val70Ub pocket, offering a promising new therapeutic strategy. powered by *this image is generated using AI for illustrative purposes only. Sunshine Biopharma Inc. and the University of Arizona have published new research findings in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry detailing the efficacy of MR1-114, a novel PLpro inhibitor, against SARS-CoV-2 variants. The study demonstrates that MR1-114 exhibits nanomolar potency in vitro against at least three variants of the virus, including the original Washington Strain, Delta, and Omicron BA.5. In vivo results from a mouse model of SARS-CoV-2 infection indicate that repeated oral administration of MR1-114 significantly suppressed pulmonary viral replication and prevented disease-associated weight loss, matching the therapeutic efficacy of Nirmatrelvir. The research highlights MR1-114's broad-spectrum activity and desirable ADME profile, including high oral bioavailability and preferential enrichment in the lungs of mice and rats. The compound targets two vulnerabilities remote from the catalytic site of the PLpro protease: the BL2 groove and the cryptic Val70Ub pocket. This approach addresses the challenge posed by PLpro's featureless active site, which has historically hindered the development of effective inhibitors. Key Findings from the Study Metric Detail Compound MR1-114 Target PLpro protease Variants Tested Washington Strain, Delta, Omicron BA.5 Potency Nanomolar in vitro Administration Oral Efficacy Comparator Nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid) Dr. Gregory Thatcher, pharmacology professor at the University of Arizona, emphasized the importance of the support from Sunshine Biopharma in exploring antiviral agents for future outbreaks. Dr. Rui Xiong, assistant professor in the Department of Pharmacology & Toxicology, noted that MR1-114 and its analogs offer a promising new strategy for targeting PLpro and could complement existing SARS-CoV-2 antivirals. Dr. Steve Slilaty, CEO of Sunshine Biopharma and co-author of the publication, expressed delight in collaborating with the University of Arizona researchers. He stated that the publication reflects the company's commitment to advancing science and improving patient outcomes, underscoring the potential of MR1-114 to transform the treatment landscape for SARS Coronavirus infections. The company looks forward to further exploring the compound's capabilities and clinical development. Sunshine Biopharma currently has 60 generic prescription drugs on the market in Canada, with approximately 12 additional drugs scheduled for launch in the remainder of 2026. Its proprietary drug development program includes K1.1 mRNA for liver cancer and the PLpro protease inhibitor for SARS Coronavirus infections. Sunshine Biopharma Inc. has received approval for its 1mg generic Anastrozole tablets for the Canadian market, expanding its portfolio of specialty prescription medications. Anastrozole is the generic equivalent of the brand name breast cancer drug Arimidex. This approval positions the company to participate in a market segment projected to grow significantly over the next decade. Anastrozole functions as a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor, lowering estrogen levels in the body to slow or reverse the growth of specific breast tumors. It serves as standard care for the adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. The drug's therapeutic application addresses a critical need in oncology treatment. Market Projections The global market for Anastrozole is expected to witness substantial growth in the coming years.
